1.pericope_label: For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob. And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place: and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors. And it shall come to pass in the day that the Lord shall give thee rest from thy sorrow, and from thy fear, and from the hard bondage wherein thou wast made to serve

schools.summary: Reads the opening as a critical hinge, since the words imply a prevision of the return and therefore of the exile, and the whole section anticipates the argument of the later chapters, so that the question of authorship stands or falls with it; presses the promise of ruling over oppressors as an ideal no historical reality has yet answered, traces successive fulfilments of the joining of strangers, and separates the words for trouble that plagues and restlessness that wears a man out.

Takes the opening particle as assigning a reason, so that Babylon falls because God will have mercy on a people he cannot reject, and draws the consolation that the whole world is governed for the salvation of the elect; treats the return as a slight foretaste only, observes what actually followed it, when the neighbouring peoples leagued to distress them, and reads the repeated confirmations as concession to a weakness that believes with difficulty when affairs contradict the promise.

Argues that the two names are used with design, each taking in all twelve tribes, and that the circumstances described did not in any complete sense accompany the return, so the whole prophecy must look beyond it; supplies a textual note that two manuscripts and the older versions restore a word to the phrase about that day, one among many instances of a word lost out of the printed copies.

Reads the tie between Babylon's fall and mercy on Jacob from the symmetry of providence, the injuries needing to be revenged and the yoke broken, so that one prediction serves as promise to the one side and threatening to the other, as the same providence had a bright face toward Israel and a dark one toward Egypt.

debates.question: How far does the prophecy reach?

positions.view: beyond the return from Babylon, since the two names are used with design, each taking in all twelve tribes, and the circumstances did not in any complete sense accompany that return

the words imply a prevision of the return and therefore of the exile, and the whole section anticipates the argument of the later chapters, so the question of its authorship stands or falls on the same grounds
the return was a slight foretaste only, all these statements being referable to Christ
a first accomplishment in the edict that sent them home and a further one in the latter day
literally at the return, and more eminently in the days of the gospel

debates.question: Has the promise that they shall rule over their oppressors ever been kept?

positions.view: the decree of return answered it in a measure, but the words paint an ideal to which no historical reality has yet corresponded, since no later period has seen this people ruling a conquered race; any real fulfilment is of the kind the Latin poet meant when captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive
in the apostles, Jews who by the word subdued the very nations to whom their people had been tributaries

debates.question: What is the day of rest, and what lay behind the hard bondage?

positions.view: the words are to be separated, one meaning trouble that plagues and another restlessness that wears a man out with care, the verb being the form commonly used for procuring rest

a monarch bent on towers and palaces who had carried off the skilled labour would vex his captives with fear and hard bondage, as an Assyrian king's own boast of making prisoners carry burdens and lay brick confirms
the repeated confirmations are a concession to our weakness, since we believe with difficulty when our affairs contradict the promise

outliers.reading: Supplies a textual note the others do not, that two manuscripts and the older versions add a word restoring the phrase about that day to the form almost always used on such occasions, and takes it for one among many instances of a word lost out of the printed copies.

Prefers to make the opening particle assign a reason rather than merely connect, so that Babylon is destroyed because God will have mercy on a people he cannot reject, and draws from it the consolation that the whole world is governed for the salvation of the elect; and observes what actually followed the return, that so far from assisting them the neighbouring peoples leagued to distress them and would have driven them out of the world.

themes: For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob.

And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place: and the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the Lord for servants and handmaids: and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors.
And it shall come to pass in the day that the Lord shall give thee rest from thy sorrow, and from thy fear, and from the hard bondage wherein thou wast made to serve,

4.pericope_label: That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased! The Lord hath broken the staff of the wicked, and the sceptre of the rulers. He who smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke is persecuted, and none hindereth. The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet: they break forth into singing. Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon

schools.summary: Specialises the generic sense of the word into a derisive utterance in poetic speech, the prophet appearing once more as a psalmist, and reports that the word for the golden city occurs nowhere else, recent critics preferring the task-master or the place of torture; distinguishes the staff a man leans on from the sceptre he wields to smite, corrects the following verse into a relative clause, identifies the tree with a pine of the Lebanon range, and calls it a distinctive peculiarity of this prophet to bring the forest in as living and speaking.

Takes the word for sayings weighty and worth observing and finds the ruin so great that it passes into a proverb, thinks the disputed name denotes the covetousness and insatiable greediness of that nation, insists the breaking was God's own act and no work of chance before which the ungodly stand bewildered, and makes the speaking trees an amplification, since men silenced under a tyrant break out when he falls and even the dumb creatures are brought in to say what the living dared not.

Makes the word the general name for Hebrew poetic style, covering the sententious, the figurative and the sublime together, notes that the Greek turns it into a lamentation and takes it for elegiac verse, reads the golden city as the coin or ingot paid over as tribute or as a name the people used of themselves, and keeps the trees themselves, felled for her pride and luxury and now suffered to stand.

Takes in the whole monarchy that sank with the last of its kings and describes the poem as prepared not to adorn a hearse but to expose the memory and fix a lasting brand of infamy on it; turns the golden city into a question, how men get wealth but by squeezing it out of others, and sets against it the one city truly golden.

debates.question: What kind of composition is the taunting song?

positions.view: the general name for Hebrew poetic style, covering the sententious, the figurative and the sublime together, so that an almost unfigurative prophecy and a long poem of another cast can both bear it; the Greek makes it a lamentation, taking it for elegiac verse of the longer sort
the generic sense specialised into a derisive utterance in poetic speech, the Greek rendering being singular
a taunting speech full of ironies, which the older versions make a mournful song, though sung by the church over her enemy it is rather a triumphant one
sayings weighty and worth observing, the ruin being so great that it passes into a proverb, the question form carrying astonishment and ridicule

debates.question: What is the golden city?

positions.view: if the English stands it matches a Greek dramatist's epithet for Babylon, but the word occurs nowhere else, and recent critics with the older versions prefer the task-master or the place of torture
the golden coin paid over as tribute
a name the people used of themselves, given here in their own tongue
a name that convicts, since men get wealth only by squeezing it out of others
rather the covetousness and insatiable greediness to which that nation was subject

debates.question: Are the rejoicing trees literal or figurative?

positions.view: a distinctive peculiarity of this prophet to bring the forest in as living and speaking
the literal and figurative senses melt into each other, since Assyrian kings boasted of felling forests wherever they conquered while the fir and cedar were also natural symbols of kingly rule
a figure of speech, or else princes comparable to such trees
the trees themselves, felled for her pride and luxury and now suffered to stand
personification for amplification, since men silenced under a tyrant break out when he falls

outliers.reading: Lays down the rule for rejoicing before joining in it, that we must not rejoice when our enemy falls as ours but when the common enemy of God and his Israel sinks; and describes the poem as prepared not to adorn a hearse or a monument but to expose the memory and fix a lasting brand of infamy on it.

Defends the scoffing against the charge that it ill suits godly modesty, since mockery is not inconsistent with compassion when the zeal is regulated by the justice of God's judgment, and as the Lord laughs at their senselessness he bids us mock, not that we may be swelled with impudence but that we may praise his goodness and power.

themes: That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased!
The Lord hath broken the staff of the wicked, and the sceptre of the rulers.
He who smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke, he that ruled the nations in anger, is persecuted, and none hindereth.
The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet: they break forth into singing.
Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us.

9.pericope_label: Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth. All they shall say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? Thy pomp is brought down to the grave: the worm is spread under thee. How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will be like the most High. Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell

schools.summary: Fills in the world below most fully, with the shades as giant-spectres of departed greatness, a masculine verb personifying the place, chief ones that are literally bell-wethers of a flock whose shepherd is death, and kings who keep their majesty on thrones apart from the vulgar dead; limits the speech of the shades to a single question of astonishment, refuses the identification of the fallen star with Satan, and denies that the mount of assembly can be Zion, which was neither a northern point of the earth nor north of the city.

Keeps the underworld a figure, speech given to the dead as gladness was given to the trees and the whole ironical, reads the question as bitter jeering since tyrants blinded by greatness think themselves half-gods until death shows how small the dimensions of men's bodies are, and sharpens the final reversal, since in a wide sepulchre the honourable dead lie in the middle while this one is thrust into a corner.

Turns the thrones of the dead into the sarcasm, graves being their only thrones now, paved and covered with worms for gold; and protests hardest against reading the fallen star as Satan, since the context speaks of a Babylonian king and it would be strange if the Spirit called the arch-enemy of God the light-bringer, the rendering itself being doubtful and perhaps meaning Howl, son of the morning.

debates.question: Who is speaking, and for how long?

positions.view: the shades say only the one question of astonishment; everything after it belongs to the singers of the song again
the vision of the spectral world ends at the same point, though the song resumed afterwards is coloured throughout by it
the dead go on speaking
the question is bitter jeering, since tyrants think themselves half-gods and death alone acknowledges how small the dimensions of men's bodies are

debates.question: Is the fallen star Satan?

positions.view: no: the context speaks of a Babylonian king, it would be strange if the Spirit called the arch-enemy of God the light-bringer, and the rendering itself is doubtful, the word coming from a root meaning to howl

no: the word is the shining one, the planet Venus, symbol of a power bound up with star-worship, and the later Latin use of the English name for the devil has hidden from most readers that a king is addressed
not to be understood of the fall of Satan, though there may be an allusion; the papal antichrist will fall from his heaven in like manner
the morning star, named in other ancient languages too from its brilliance, the title son of the dawn answering to a classical parentage

debates.question: What is the mount of the assembly?

positions.view: the mount of the divine presence, so named not because the people gathered there but because God appointed it as his meeting-place, the stars of God being the Israelites
the temple hill, the north being exact since it lay northward of Zion strictly so called

not Jerusalem at all: most modern scholars hold that reading untenable, and what is meant is the heaven where the gods the king believed in sat in council, as Assyrian hymns speak of feasts in the silver mountains
it cannot be Zion, which was neither a northern point of the earth nor north of the city; the mistake rests on a misunderstood psalm

outliers.reading: Sharpens the closing reversal beyond the others, since the king had meant to set his throne above the clouds and will be given a corner of a sepulchre instead: in a wide tomb the honourable dead are laid in the middle, and this one is thrust into the edge.

Finds indignant sarcasm in the repetition of the word for recesses, since the proud king does reach the recesses he had spoken of, only they are in the pit and not in heaven; and identifies the chief ones of the earth as literally the bell-wethers of a flock whose shepherd is death, the kings keeping their old majesty on thrones apart from the vulgar dead.

themes: Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations.
All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?
Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee.
How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north:
I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High.
Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.

16.pericope_label: They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that made the world as a wilderness, and opened not the house of his prisoners? All the kings of the nations lie in glory, every one in his own house. But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch. Thou shalt not be joined with them in burial, because thou hast destroyed thy land, and slain thy people

schools.summary: Shifts the scene from the shadow-world to the field of battle where men gaze at the conqueror's corpse, prefers the marginal reading that he loosed not his prisoners to their homes and documents it from Assyrian kings who kept captive kings chained like dogs in the palace court, contrasts the sepulchres of other monarchs, called an eternal home and often almost literally the palace of the dead, and closes from a Sidonian tomb-curse that joins the two halves of this sentence exactly.

Keeps the whole discourse in the mouth of the dead, explains the gazing itself, since men stretch the neck at anything strange, refuses to limit the prophecy to one king because history does not show the greatest of them denied burial, and defends burial as a custom held sacred in all ages and a symbol of the resurrection, before turning it into justice: the man who laid the earth desolate does not deserve that she receive him into her bosom.

Takes the cast-out body for the tree abominated, the wood on which a malefactor was hanged, which a Jewish authority says was buried with him lest it keep an ill name, as the stone that stoned him and the sword that killed him were; and applies the denial of burial to the last king of the line, whose people would have had neither opportunity nor heart to bury him honourably.

debates.question: Who is looking narrowly at him?

positions.view: the living, on a battlefield; the scene has shifted from the shadow-world, and men gaze at the corpse as it lies dishonoured, bloody and unburied
the dead still; the words might be referred to the living, but the whole discourse is better kept in their mouth

debates.question: Does the prophecy fit the greatest king of Babylon?

positions.view: no, and this is the reason for not limiting it to one man, since history does not show that king denied burial, the Jewish story that his son had him dug up being treated as a fable even by a credulous father; a whole dynasty is described
relates the same Jewish story at length as the Jews tell it
it fits the last of the line, whose people would have had neither opportunity nor heart to bury him honourably
the contrast is the point: every other king was laid out within his own palace, while this one lay far from the sepulchre meant for him

debates.question: What is the abominable branch?

positions.view: the tree abominated, the wood on which a malefactor was hanged, buried with him lest it keep an ill name
a scion mildewed and blasted which men fling away as loathsome
a rotten twig the pruner throws aside

outliers.reading: Answers the question the others do not raise, why the want of a grave should count as a curse: burial is not necessary to salvation, yet to be denied it is justly a disgrace, the value set on it among all nations coming from the patriarchs whose bodies God commanded to be buried in hope of the resurrection, so that where the carcases of beasts are cast out as fit only to rot, ours are laid in the earth to be kept against the last day.

Documents the cruelty charged from the monuments, since Assyrian kings boast of carrying captive kings off in chains of iron and keeping them chained like dogs in the palace court, one held thirty-seven years; and closes from a Sidonian king's tomb-curse that joins the two halves of this sentence exactly, no couch among the shades, no grave, no son or seed in his stead.

themes: They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms;
That made the world as a wilderness, and destroyed the cities thereof; that opened not the house of his prisoners?
All the kings of the nations, even all of them, lie in glory, every one in his own house.

But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet.
Thou shalt not be joined with them in burial, because thou hast destroyed thy land, and slain thy people: the seed of evildoers shall never be renowned.

21.pericope_label: Prepare slaughter for his children for the iniquity of their fathers; that they do not rise, nor possess the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. For I will rise up against them, saith the Lord of hosts, and cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew, saith the Lord. I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction

schools.summary: Allows the Medes if any particular persons were in the prophet's mind, reads the negative particle as a wish that no Babylonian kingdom should ever arise again, and adds from an inscription that a later pretender took the great name falsely while the last shoot of the royal house was killed as a conspirator's child; declines the proposed emendations of the clause about cities, argues for a water bird from the word's company, and supplies the mechanism of the flooding, the waters held off by artificial defences now let loose.

Makes the executioners a body held in readiness, Medes and Persians and others, since the city was not wholly destroyed when the Persians took it, observes that God now says he will do himself what he had commanded others to do, which shows both that the ruin of the wicked is his own work and how far prophecy carries, and reasons from the word's company that the creature is one found near water, which suits a site lying moist though not marshy between two great rivers.

Follows the Greek into another image, plunging the city in a miry gulf rather than sweeping it, observes that the prophet writing to Chaldeans uses words peculiar to their own tongue for the divine judgments, reports a large body of manuscripts reading the plural, and takes the creature for a fowl delighting in solitary watery ground.

debates.question: Who is commanded to prepare the slaughter?

positions.view: the Medes, if any particular persons were in mind at all

the Medes, or any minister of the divine vengeance; in the judgment of God as history shows it the stroke falls of necessity on the last members of a cruel dynasty, while behind the veil each soul stands on its own responsibility
executioners held in readiness, Medes and Persians and others, since the city was not wholly destroyed when the Persians took it

debates.question: What creature takes possession of the ruins?

positions.view: a water fowl that makes a horrible noise by putting its bill into mire, though owl, osprey, tortoise, beaver and hedgehog have all been proposed

naturalists are not agreed, but the word stands elsewhere beside the pelican and here beside pools, while the hedgehog keeps to dry places and does not roost on ruined capitals, so bittern may as well stand
an animal found near water is probable from the connection, which suits a site lying moist though not marshy between two great rivers
a fowl delighting in solitary watery ground such as lay about Babylon

debates.question: What is the besom of destruction?

positions.view: not a besom at all; following the Greek, a plunging of the city in a miry gulf, and a large body of manuscripts reads the plural besides
the English should stand and the force of the image be felt, since Babylon is swept away as men sweep foul rubbish from a house, and the world is cleaner for its destruction
the mechanism is the point: the waters held off by artificial defences are let loose, so the river without its dam lays the region under water

outliers.reading: Lists the emendations proposed for the clause about filling the world with cities, ruined heaps, terrible ones, enemies, conflicts, and declines them all, since the words describe the boast of monarchs who built cities to perpetuate their fame, the Assyrian and Babylonian kings recording their building and their destroying with equal exultation; he notes too that the heaped words for descent, with the term for nephew in its true sense of grandson, carry the emphasis of alliteration, as our own bag and baggage does.

Observes that God now declares he will do himself what he had just commanded others to do, which shows both that the ruin of wicked men is his own work though he employs human agency, and how far prophecy carries, the prophets by it commanding nations.

themes: Prepare slaughter for his children for the iniquity of their fathers; that they do not rise, nor possess the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities.
For I will rise up against them, saith the Lord of hosts, and cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew, saith the Lord.
I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the Lord of hosts.

24.pericope_label: The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand: that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and upon my mountains tread him under foot. This is the purpose that is purposed upon the whole earth: and this is the hand that is stretched out upon all the nations. For the Lord of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it?

schools.summary: Calls the Assyrian passage a fragmentary prophecy, possibly misplaced and possibly added as proof that what was fulfilled on Assyria would be fulfilled on Babylon, the two being almost identified in the prophet's thought, finds the fulfilment in the destruction of the invader's army on hills called God's own because they were sacred to him, and takes the closing verses as pointing to a universal history, the last clause reading more emphatically his is the outstretched hand.

Makes the oath a remedy for a particular weakness, since nothing is harder to believe than the sudden ruin of men we see flourishing, presses the broken form of the words as a deliberate check on our own freedom with oaths, will not fix the date but conjectures the slaughter had already happened, and answers both the charge that the Spirit uses too many words and the objection that God has changed his purpose.

Takes the two peoples for one on the authority of two ancient geographers while allowing that the judgment on God's own mountains may point to the destruction near Jerusalem and have a farther view, and keeps the reference of the closing verses nearer, to the vast empire now held by one power and shortly to pass to another.

Supplies the pastoral reason for the turn, since the fall of Babylon lay almost two hundred years off and the hearers might ask what it was to them and what assurance they had of it, so the ruin of the enemies then at their door is given as a present comfort and a pledge for their posterity; and adds the moral that those who wrongfully invade God's land find it is at their peril.

debates.question: Why does the oracle turn to Assyria here?

positions.view: it is a fragmentary prophecy, possibly misplaced, possibly added as proof that what was fulfilled on Assyria would be fulfilled on Babylon too
because the fall of Babylon lay almost two hundred years off, and the ruin of the enemies then at their door is given as a present comfort and a pledge for their posterity
as a proof of favour held out against the objection that the ruin of Babylon can do nothing for a people Babylon has already ruined

debates.question: Is the Assyrian of this passage Babylon under another name?

positions.view: either that, though the king of Babylon did not fall in the land of Israel, or more likely a return to the earlier prophecy about the invader, which some read as already past
the two peoples are one on the authority of two ancient geographers, though the judgment on God's mountains may point to the destruction near Jerusalem and have a farther view
the words found their fulfilment in the destruction of the invader's army, the mountains being the hills round the city where it lay encamped
the date cannot be fixed, but the slaughter had probably already happened, so the prophet argues from a known deliverance to a future one

debates.question: What does the oath itself teach?

positions.view: his word is his oath, so the Greek gives only thus saith the Lord; the addition is made for his people's comfort
it is needed because nothing is harder to believe than the ruin of men we see flourishing, and its broken form is deliberate, a check on our own freedom with oaths

outliers.reading: Answers two objections at once out of the repetition: to the charge that the prophet, or rather the Spirit, uses too many words, that those who think so are not well acquainted with themselves, since the two things set before us, purpose and power, answer to the two causes of unbelief; and to the objection that God has changed his purpose, as when he spared a repenting city, that what was preached there was not the secret decree but a word meant to rouse them.

Takes the closing verses as pointing to the idea of a universal history, since the fall of Assyria and of Babylon does not stand alone but forms part of a scheme embracing all nations and all ages; and sharpens the last clause, which reads more emphatically his is the outstretched hand.

themes: The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand:
That I will break the Assyrian in my land, and upon my mountains tread him under foot: then shall his yoke depart from off them, and his burden depart from off their shoulders.
This is the purpose that is purposed upon the whole earth: and this is the hand that is stretched out upon all the nations.
For the Lord of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? and his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?

28.pericope_label: In the year that king Ahaz died was this burden. Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent’s root shall come forth a cockatrice. And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the needy shall lie down in safety. Howl, O gate; cry, O city; for there shall come from the north a smoke. What shall one then answer the messengers of the nation? That the Lord hath founded Zion

schools.summary: Notes that the date is fixed either by the prophet or by his compiler so that it might be seen the words were not written after the event, makes the broken rod either the Davidic sceptre shattered in the Syro-Ephraimite war or the power of the Assyrian king, gives the smoke from the north to the Assyrians and probably to their torch-signals, and suspects that the whole series of oracles following was delivered in answer to inquiries from other nations.

Protests that the fifteenth chapter ought to have begun here, since a new subject opens and the divisions are not so much made as torn asunder, refers the broken rod to the older king and then beyond him, one man standing for the whole body of the people, calls the poor eminent for wretchedness and holding first rank among the wretched, and reads the smoke as standing for the fire that follows it.

Divides over the broken rod, one voice giving it to the king who had subdued the Philistines two reigns before and making his house the serpent's root, the other rejecting both that king, dead thirty-two years, and the late king, who was smitten rather than smiting, in favour of a royal race whose sceptre had passed to slothful princes; the smoke is taken for a dust-cloud raised by a marching army, or for Chaldea and a grievous judgment.

Closes on the answer rather than the question, that Zion was founded as a refuge for the poor who flee from the wrath to come, and turns it into exhortation, that we should tell all around of our comforts and security and urge them to seek the same refuge.

debates.question: Whose rod was broken?

positions.view: the king who had subdued the Philistines two reigns before, the serpent's root being his house, from which a far more terrible enemy would come

neither that king, dead thirty-two years so that joy at his death was long past, nor the late king, who was smitten rather than smiting, but the royal race itself, whose sceptre had passed to slothful princes
the Davidic sceptre, which had held the Philistines down and was shattered by the war with Syria and Ephraim; the phrase means the rod which smote thee rather than the rod of him that smote thee
the power of the Assyrian king, in whose death, or in that of Ahaz, the Philistines were exulting
the older king, but not he alone, since one man stands for the whole body of the people

debates.question: Whose smoke comes from the north?

positions.view: no smoke at all, but a cloud of dust raised by the march of the Judean army, since a great dust at a distance looks like smoke
the Assyrian invaders, the smoke being either burning cities or, likelier, the torch-signals used on night marches, so that the last clause means there is no straggler at the appointed places
the smoke stands for the fire that follows it; either the Assyrians or the Jews may be meant, both lying northward, though the Jews are likelier
Chaldea, and a grievous judgment; not one of that army will desert his colours

debates.question: Who asks the closing question?

positions.view: ambassadors of the surrounding nations coming to congratulate a victory, or, if the singular of the text stands, envoys of the Philistines suing for peace
the verse implies an inquiry received or expected, and the whole series of oracles following may have been delivered in answer to such inquiries, the prophet's fame having spread beyond Israel
not the messengers sent to Hezekiah but such as were sent to him in congratulation

outliers.reading: Protests at the chapter division before treating the prophecy at all, holding that the fifteenth chapter ought to have begun here since a new subject opens, and that this plainly shows how absurdly the chapters are divided, or rather torn asunder.

Closes on the answer rather than the question, that the Lord founded Zion as a refuge for poor sinners who flee from the wrath to come and trust his mercy, and turns it into exhortation, that we should tell all around of our comforts and security and urge them to seek the same refuge and salvation.

themes: In the year that king Ahaz died was this burden.
Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent’s root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent.
And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the needy shall lie down in safety: and I will kill thy root with famine, and he shall slay thy remnant.
Howl, O gate; cry, O city; thou, whole Palestina, art dissolved: for there shall come from the north a smoke, and none shall be alone in his appointed times.
What shall one then answer the messengers of the nation? That the Lord hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it.
